previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for chest and abdominal pain following a motor vehicle collision ten days prior. Chest pain was determined to be non-cardiac, likely musculoskeletal, with normal troponins, EKG changes not indicative of acute ischemia, and a clear chest X-ray. Abdominal pain was consistent with a flare of chronic pancreatitis, managed with NPO status, IV fluids, and pain control. IV Dilaudid was used initially, then transitioned to oral tramadol as tolerated. A central line was placed for medication access. Psychiatry was consulted to support pain and medication management given the patient's history. The patient improved over seven days, advanced to a regular diet, and was discharged on oral tramadol, home medications, and vitamin D supplementation. Follow-up was arranged with pain, psychiatric, and primary care providers.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ year old female with a history multiple admissions for 
depression (with suicide attempt), chronic pain, numerous 
admissions for chronic pancreatitis marked by inability to 
tolerate PO s/p J-tube placement who is now presenting with 
""typical pancreatitis pain"" and non-exertional chest pain which 
radiates down the left arm and is exacerbated by nausea, 
vomiting and pain. The patient was subsequently admitted for 
hydration, pain control, and workup of chest pain. 

1. Atypical Chest pain: 

The patient noted new onset left retrosternal chest pain which 
radiated down her left arm. This pain was not associated with 
exertion and was not relieved with rest. The patient noted that 
this pain was exacerbated by nausea and vomiting. She also 
stated that the pain was relieved by sublingual nitroglycerine. 
Her EKG was normal and did not show changes consistent with 
ischemia compared to previous EKGS. She had two negative sets of 
cardiac enzymes. The fact that her pain was relieved by SLN is 
suggestive that the patient might have diffuse esophageal spasm. 
However, after hospital day one, despite nausea and vomiting, 
the patient did not experience any more chest pain. She required 
no further sublingual nitroglycerine. 

2. Chronic pancreatitis: This was the patient's ___ medical 
admission in the last 12 months or so (most admissions are for 
the same abdominal pain).  Patient had symptoms of nausea, 
vomiting, and abdominal pain. On this admission, her LFTs were 
elevated but pancreatic enzymes were normal.

radiology_notes.text:
PICC LINE PLACEMENT

INDICATION:  IV access needed for antibiotics.

The procedure was explained to the patient.  A timeout was performed.

RADIOLOGIST:  Dr. ___ (fellow) performed the procedure.  Dr.
___ (attending physician) was present and supervised throughout
the procedure.

TECHNIQUE:  Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the right brachial
vein was punctured under direct ultrasound guidance using a micropuncture set.
Hard copies of ultrasound images were obtained before and immediately after
establishing intravenous access.  A peel-away sheath was then placed over a
guidewire and a double-lumen PICC line measuring 43 cm in length was then
placed through the peel-away sheath with its tip positioned in the SVC under
fluoroscopic guidance.  Position of the catheter was confirmed by a
fluoroscopic spot film of the chest.

The peel-away sheath and guidewire were then removed.  The catheter was
secured to the skin, flushed, and a sterile dressing applied.

The patient tolerated the procedure well.  There were no immediate
complications.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated ultrasound and fluoroscopically guided 5 ___
double-lumen PICC line placement via the right brachial venous approach. 
Final internal length is 43 cm, with the tip positioned in SVC.  The line is
ready to use.
